stem: With the spectacles placed temples-away so the back surface rests on the lens stop, which power does a manual lensmeter read?
choices: Equivalent power measured from the principal planes
Front vertex power
Nominal power (the sum of the two surface powers)
Back vertex power
explanation: The lensmeter's field lens puts its focal point at the back surface of the lens being read, so the instrument reports back vertex power, the reciprocal of the back focal length. That is the power that matters for the eye behind the lens.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Before reading any lens, how should the lensmeter eyepiece be focused?
choices: With no lens in place, turn it fully toward plus to blur the reticle, then turn slowly back just until the reticle clears
With no lens in place, turn it fully toward minus, then back toward plus until the reticle clears
Leave it at the factory zero; the eyepiece is not user-adjustable
With the patient's lens in place, rock it back and forth until the mires look sharpest
explanation: Fogging the eyepiece in the plus direction and then backing off only until the reticle is clear focuses it for the examiner's eye while keeping accommodation relaxed. Check this every time the instrument is used.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Why should you stop turning the eyepiece the moment the reticle first comes into focus?
choices: It moves the lens stop off the optical axis
It rescales the prism rings
Turning past that point lets your own accommodation enter the reading
Turning further shifts the axis protractor
explanation: Once the reticle is just clear, any extra turn makes the eyepiece too minus for a relaxed eye. You then accommodate to keep the reticle sharp, and that accommodation skews the power readings.

source.title: Lensometry – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: After focusing the eyepiece with no lens in place, the mires come into focus at +0.25 D instead of zero. What is the correct response?
choices: Accept it, because 0.25 D is within tolerance
Refocus the eyepiece; if the mires still don't focus at plano, have the instrument recalibrated
Rotate the axis wheel 90° and refocus
Subtract 0.25 D from every reading
explanation: With no lens in place, the mires should focus at a drum reading of zero. If they don't, repeat the eyepiece procedure. A persistent offset means the lensmeter needs calibration; don't correct readings in your head.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: When positioning the spectacles on a manual lensmeter, what is the standard orientation?
choices: Temples facing the operator, front surface against the lens stop
Temples pointing straight up, lens held at 90° to the stop
Temples facing away from the operator, back surface against the lens stop
Either way, because both orientations give the same reading for every lens
explanation: Temples-away puts the back surface on the stop so the instrument reads back vertex power, which is the correct surface for most measurements.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: Why should the bottoms of both eyewires rest evenly on the spectacle table while you read a lens?
choices: It keeps the lens stop from scratching the coating
It sets the vertex distance for the reading
It centers the bifocal segment automatically
It keeps the frame's 180° line level, so axis and prism readings aren't rotated
explanation: If the frame tips on the table, the lens rotates with it. The cylinder axis and the prism base direction then read off by the same amount.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: In plus-cylinder technique on a crossed-line (American cross) target, where along the power drum do the sphere (single) lines come into focus?
choices: At the most plus reading of the two
At the least plus (most minus) reading of the two
At whichever reading is closer to plano
At the same reading as the cylinder lines, for any spherocylinder
explanation: In plus-cylinder technique you work from high minus toward plus. The sphere lines focus first, at the less plus power. The cylinder lines focus later in the plus direction, so the difference is a plus cylinder.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Working in plus-cylinder technique, you turn the drum from high minus toward plus and the thick cylinder lines come into focus before the thin sphere lines. What should you do?
choices: Rotate the axis wheel 90° and start again
Record a minus cylinder at the current axis
Record the thick-line reading as the sphere
Turn the eyepiece toward plus and refocus
explanation: If the cylinder lines focus first, the target is set 90° from the plus-cylinder axis. Rotating the axis wheel 90° brings the sphere lines in first so the second reading gives a plus cylinder.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: In plus-cylinder technique, the sphere lines are sharp and unbroken at −2.00 with the axis wheel at 090. Turning toward plus, the cylinder lines focus at −0.75. What is the lens power?
explanation: Sphere = first reading = −2.00. Cylinder = second − first = −0.75 − (−2.00) = +1.25. Axis = 090 from the wheel. In minus cylinder this is −0.75 −1.25 × 180.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: A lens reads −2.00 +1.25 × 090 in plus-cylinder form. How should it be written in minus-cylinder form?
explanation: To transpose, add the cylinder to the sphere (−2.00 + 1.25 = −0.75), change the cylinder's sign, and rotate the axis 90° (090 → 180).

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: On the power drum number line, the first (sphere-line) reading is −2.00 and the second (cylinder-line) reading is +1.00. What is the cylinder power?
explanation: Cylinder is the distance traveled along the number line between the two readings. From −2.00 to +1.00 is three units in the plus direction, so +3.00 D.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: On a crossed-line lensmeter target, how do you recognize a spherical lens?
choices: The lines focus only after the axis wheel is turned 90°
The thin lines focus but the thick lines never do
The target can't be centered on the reticle
The thin and thick lines come into focus at the same drum reading
explanation: A sphere has the same power in every meridian, so both sets of lines sharpen at once. If they focus at different readings, the lens has cylinder.

source.title: Lensometry – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: Reading a lined bifocal, the distance sphere lines focus at −4.00. With the segment centered, the sphere lines refocus at −1.75. What is the add?
explanation: The add is the algebraic difference between the near and distance sphere readings: −1.75 − (−4.00) = +2.25. Adds are always recorded as plus.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: When measuring the add of a spherocylindrical multifocal, which lines do you refocus through the segment?
choices: Both sets, after turning the axis wheel 90°
Only the sphere (single) lines, leaving the axis wheel where it was for distance
Only the cylinder (triple) lines
Whichever set happens to focus first
explanation: The add is spherical and is the difference between the distance and near sphere readings. Leave the axis setting from distance and refocus only the single lines.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: According to standard lensometry teaching, when should a bifocal add be read with the spectacles turned around so the front vertex power is measured?
choices: For every minus-powered lens
Only for progressive lenses
When the add is high (greater than about +2.50 D)
Never; adds are always read with the temples away
explanation: A front-surface segment acts on diverging light from the near object. For strong adds, the back-vertex reading departs noticeably from the true add, so high adds are verified at the front vertex.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: If a strong front-surface bifocal add is read only as back vertex power, how does the reading compare with the true add?
choices: It reads the same at any add strength
It reads weaker than the true add
It reads as a plus cylinder
It reads stronger than the true add
explanation: Iowa's lensometry guide notes that higher bifocal powers read more powerful than they are when back vertex is used instead of front vertex. That is why high adds are rechecked with the glasses turned around.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Reading a RIGHT lens, the center of the target lands on the second ring, displaced toward the wearer's temple. What prism is present at that point?
choices: 1Δ base out
2Δ base in
4Δ base out
2Δ base out
explanation: Each reticle ring is 1Δ, and the base points the way the target is displaced. Toward the temple is base out, so this is 2Δ BO.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Reading a LEFT lens, the target center sits three rings from the reticle center toward the wearer's nose. What is recorded?
choices: 3Δ base down
1.5Δ base in
3Δ base in
3Δ base out
explanation: Displacement toward the nose means base in, whichever eye you are reading. Three rings is 3Δ.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: The target center is displaced straight down, halfway between the first and second rings. What prism does the lens have at that point?
choices: 1.5Δ base down
3Δ base down
0.5Δ base down
1.5Δ base up
explanation: Downward displacement means base down. Halfway between ring 1 and ring 2 is 1.5Δ.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: The target is off the reticle field. Holding a 6Δ base-in loose prism over the lens brings it back to center. How much prism is in the lens?
choices: 12Δ base in
6Δ base out
6Δ base in
3Δ base out
explanation: A loose prism that neutralizes the lens's prism has to be oriented opposite to it. If 6Δ BI centers the target, the lens contains 6Δ BO.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: A lens contains more prism than the reticle rings can show (well over 5Δ). Which method lets you measure it on a manual lensmeter?
choices: Use the prism compensating device or hold auxiliary loose prisms to bring the target back to center
Refocus the eyepiece in the plus direction until the target reappears
Record the reading as 'over 5Δ'
Decenter the lens until the target appears and record no prism
explanation: The rings only cover about 5Δ. Beyond that, add a known amount of opposing prism (a PCD or loose prisms) until the target is centered, then read the amount and direction.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: What is the most reliable way to find out whether a patient's single-vision glasses are inducing prism by decentration?
choices: Center each lens on its optical center and read the rings
Compare the frame PD with the patient's PD on the order form
Read the lenses on an automated lensmeter in progressive mode
Mark each pupil center on the lenses while the patient wears the glasses, then center those marks on the lens stop
explanation: If you simply center each lens, you will always find the optical center and see no prism. Reading at the marked pupil locations shows the prism the patient actually looks through.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: A right lens is +4.00 D sphere. The wearer's pupil mark is 3 mm nasal to the optical center. What prism does the patient look through?
choices: 12Δ base out
1.2Δ base out
0.75Δ base out
1.2Δ base in
explanation: Prentice's rule: P = D × d(cm) = 4.00 × 0.3 = 1.2Δ. In a plus lens the base points toward the optical center. Here the OC is temporal to the pupil, so the prism is base out.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: A −5.00 D sphere has its optical center 2 mm above the wearer's pupil mark. What vertical prism is at the pupil?
choices: 1.0Δ base up
0.4Δ base down
1.0Δ base down
10Δ base down
explanation: P = 5.00 × 0.2 = 1.0Δ. In a minus lens the base points away from the optical center. The OC is above the pupil, so the base is down.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: With the lens positioned so the target crosses at the center of the reticle, the marking device dots the lens. What does the center dot locate?
choices: The geometric center of the lens shape
The patient's pupil center
The lens's optical center
The fitting cross of a progressive
explanation: When the target is centered, the lens has no prism at the spot over the lens stop. By definition that spot is the optical center, and the marker dots it.

source.title: Lensometry – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: Where should the add of a progressive lens be read on a lensmeter?
choices: At the fitting cross
Anywhere along the corridor, since the power is constant there
At the prism reference point
In the near reference area, as low in the lens as practical, avoiding the distorted periphery
explanation: Power keeps increasing down the corridor and the periphery is distorted, so read the add through the near area low in the lens and choose the least-distorted spot.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: At which point on a progressive lens is the prism verified?
choices: The fitting cross
The prism reference point (PRP)
The distance reference circle
The near reference circle
explanation: Prism in a progressive is measured at the prism reference point. Its target displacement there gives the prism amount and base direction.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Where is the prism reference point of a progressive lens normally found?
choices: Midway between the two permanent engraved circles, a few millimeters below the fitting cross
At the fitting cross itself
At the center of the near reference circle
Inside the distance reference circle above the fitting cross
explanation: The PRP sits halfway between the factory engravings, typically 2–4 mm below the fitting cross. Find the engravings first, then mark the PRP.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: By international standard, how far apart are the two permanent alignment engravings on a progressive lens?
choices: 40 mm
34 mm
24 mm
17 mm
explanation: The two identical alignment marks are set 34 mm apart. They are used to lay the lens off horizontally and to restore the removable markings.

source.title: Hidden Markings on Progressive Power Lenses – ABDO

stem: On most progressive lenses, where is the add power engraved?
choices: Beneath the temporal alignment engraving
In the center of the near circle
Inside the fitting cross
Beneath the nasal alignment engraving
explanation: The temporal engraving typically carries the add. The nasal engraving identifies the design and often the index.

source.title: Hidden Markings on Progressive Power Lenses – ABDO

stem: A progressive lens has the hidden engraving "20" under the temporal circle. What does it most likely indicate?
choices: A 2.0 mm center thickness
A 20 mm corridor length
A +2.00 add
Index 1.620
explanation: The add is abbreviated on the lens. For example, "22" means +2.25 and "20" means +2.00.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: What is "restoring" the markings on a progressive lens?
choices: Re-engraving the lens with a laser in the office
Re-coating the lens so the engravings disappear
Reading the add with the glasses turned around
Finding and dotting the permanent engravings, then using the manufacturer's chart to relocate the fitting cross and reference points
explanation: The engravings are semi-visible. Dot them with a marker and lay the lens on the maker's centration chart to put back the fitting cross, PRP, and reference circles.

source.title: Hidden Markings on Progressive Power Lenses – ABDO

stem: A free-form (digital) progressive reads slightly different from the ordered Rx on the lensmeter. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The lensmeter is calibrated for index 1.53
The lens was edged off axis
The design is compensated for position of wear, so the lensmeter reading is not meant to match the ordered Rx exactly
The eyepiece was focused in the minus direction
explanation: Digital lenses are calculated for how the wearer sees through each part of the lens. The lensmeter reading therefore differs from the written Rx. Check against the lab's compensated values, not the raw Rx.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Which statement about automated lensmeters is accurate?
choices: They can't measure progressive lenses
They detect prism but can misread large amounts (over about 5Δ), so suspicious results should be rechecked on a manual instrument
They always read front vertex power
They are more accurate than a manual lensmeter for every lens
explanation: Automated lensmeters are fast and repeatable, but they can mismeasure large prism. When a reading doesn't fit the prescription, verify it manually.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Besides sphere, cylinder, axis, add, and prism, which additional measurement do many automated lensmeters offer?
choices: UV transmittance of the lens
Abbe value of the material
Refractive index of the material
Base curve of the front surface
explanation: Current automated lensmeters such as the Marco LM-1800 add features like automatic lens-type detection, PD measurement, and UV transmittance readout.

source.title: LM-1800/1800PD Automated Lensmeter – Marco

stem: What is the main practical tradeoff of an automated lensmeter compared with a manual one?
choices: It can only read single-vision lenses
It is more accurate but requires focusing the eyepiece for each operator
It reads front vertex power, so adds must always be recalculated
It is faster and easier to operate but considered less accurate in some cases
explanation: Automated units measure all values in one operation and display them digitally. EyeWiki notes they are easier to operate but relatively less accurate than a manual lensmeter.

source.title: Lensometry – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: Which index of refraction is a standard optician's lens clock (Geneva lens measure) calibrated for?
explanation: The standard Geneva lens measure reads in diopters for an index of 1.53. Some versions intended for crown glass are marked 1.523. On any other material, correct the reading.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: What does a lens clock physically measure?
choices: The back vertex power of the lens
The refractive index of the lens material
The sagittal depth of the surface between its fixed outer pins and the movable center pin
The thickness of the lens at its center
explanation: The center pin's travel relative to the two fixed pins is the sagitta over a known chord. The dial converts that sag to diopters using the index the gauge is calibrated for.

source.title: A Lens Gauge is a Beautiful Thing – OptikConEd (ABO-approved CE)

stem: A 1.53-calibrated lens clock reads +6.00 D on the front of a 1.66 high-index lens. What is the true surface power?
choices: About +4.75 D
About +7.50 D
About +6.75 D
explanation: True power = reading × (n − 1) / (1.53 − 1) = 6.00 × 0.66 / 0.53 ≈ +7.47 D, or about +7.50. A higher-index material has more power for the same curvature.

source.title: A Lens Gauge is a Beautiful Thing – OptikConEd (ABO-approved CE)

stem: A 1.53-calibrated lens clock reads −4.00 D on the back of a polycarbonate (n = 1.586) lens. What is the true surface power?
choices: About −4.42 D
About −3.62 D
About −5.17 D
explanation: True = −4.00 × 0.586 / 0.53 ≈ −4.42 D. The reading understates the power of any material with an index above 1.53.

source.title: A Lens Gauge is a Beautiful Thing – OptikConEd (ABO-approved CE)

stem: A 1.53 lens clock reads +8.00 D on the front of a CR-39 (n = 1.498) lens. Compared with the dial reading, the true surface power is:
choices: Slightly more, about +8.50 D
About +5.30 D
Slightly less, about +7.52 D
Exactly +8.00 D
explanation: True = 8.00 × 0.498 / 0.53 ≈ +7.52 D. A material with an index below the calibration index has less power than the dial shows.

source.title: Lens clock – Wikipedia

stem: A thin lens made of 1.53 material clocks +5.00 D on the front and −7.25 D on the back. What is its approximate (nominal) power?
explanation: For a thin lens, nominal power ≈ F1 + F2 = +5.00 + (−7.25) = −2.25 D. Thickness is ignored in this approximation.

source.title: A Lens Gauge is a Beautiful Thing – OptikConEd (ABO-approved CE)

stem: Rotating a lens clock on a back surface, the needle swings between −6.00 D and −8.50 D at positions 90° apart. What does this show?
choices: A toric surface with 2.50 D of surface cylinder
A spherical surface; the swing is normal pin play
Warpage that has added 8.50 D of power
An aspheric surface with 14.50 D of asphericity
explanation: Two stable readings 90° apart are the surface's principal meridians. The difference between them, 8.50 − 6.00 = 2.50 D, is the surface cylinder.

source.title: A Lens Gauge is a Beautiful Thing – OptikConEd (ABO-approved CE)

stem: Why are lens clock readings unreliable on progressive and aspheric surfaces?
choices: The gauge is calibrated only for minus surfaces
Those lenses are always made of polycarbonate
Their hard coats push the center pin out
The gauge assumes a single spherical curve across its three pins, so a changing curvature can clock almost the same as a sphere
explanation: A three-point gauge only matches pin depths. An asphere or a small steeper zone can sit on the pins almost exactly like a sphere, so the dial can't capture the true curvature.

source.title: Back To Basics: Understanding the Use and Limitations of a Lens Measure – 20/20 Magazine

stem: How do you check a lens clock's zero before use?
choices: Read a plano lens on the lensmeter first
Press it on a known +6.00 D lens
Hold it pins-up and check the needle
Press it on a flat surface, such as plate glass; it should read zero
explanation: A flat surface has no sag, so a calibrated clock reads zero. If it doesn't, adjust the center pin before measuring lenses.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: Lens calipers on a plano plastic lens read 3.0 mm at the center. What is this consistent with?
choices: A lens that fails the FDA drop-ball test
Standard dress thickness for any plastic lens
Safety-thickness lenses (about 3 mm) rather than standard dress thickness (about 2 mm)
A reading taken off-center that should be ignored
explanation: Calipers read in tenths of a millimeter. They are used to check whether lenses were made at standard (about 2 mm) or safety (about 3 mm) thickness.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: What does a lens circumference gauge measure, and when is it most useful?
choices: The frame's A and B dimensions, for minimum blank size
The perimeter (C-size) of an edged lens, used to size lenses accurately when the frame can't be sent to the lab
The base curve, for matching a second pair
The lens's center thickness, for safety verification
explanation: Circumference measurers wrap a calibrated tape around the edged lens. Labs consider C-size an accurate way to finish lenses to size without the frame.

source.title: Question about lens circumference – OptiBoard

stem: An optician files the polished edge of a rimless lens to reduce shine. Which measurement is most at risk?
choices: The lens circumference (C-size), which can become too small for the mounting
The cylinder axis
The base curve
The lens's back vertex power
explanation: Removing edge material shrinks the perimeter. Too much leaves the lens undersized for the frame, so work carefully or ask the lab.

source.title: Polished Lens Edges, Friend or Foe? – 20/20 Magazine

stem: When measuring the patient's RIGHT monocular PD with a millimeter rule, what does the examiner do?
choices: Closes their own left eye and has the patient look into the examiner's open right eye
Closes their own right eye and has the patient look into the examiner's left eye
Keeps both eyes open while the patient looks over the examiner's shoulder
Has the patient close the left eye and look at the ceiling
explanation: The examiner's open eye sits directly in front of the patient's eye being measured, so the patient's line of sight is straight ahead. Then reverse for the left eye.

source.title: Agreement and inter-session repeatability of manual and automatic interpupillary distance measurements – PMC

stem: Where should a PD rule be held when measuring a patient's PD?
choices: On the patient's cheeks below the lower lids
Resting on the bridge of the nose, roughly in the spectacle plane, and kept straight and level
At arm's length, halfway between examiner and patient
Against the patient's forehead above the brows
explanation: Holding the rule at about the plane the lenses will occupy, and keeping it level, reduces parallax and tilt error.

source.title: Agreement and inter-session repeatability of manual and automatic interpupillary distance measurements – PMC

stem: A corneal-reflection pupillometer aligns with the corneal reflex rather than the pupil center. Compared with a pupil-center PD, what does a binocular reflex PD typically read?
choices: About 2 mm wider
Exactly the same
About 2 mm narrower
About 6 mm narrower
explanation: The corneal reflex sits about 1 mm nasal to each pupil center at the spectacle plane, so the binocular value is typically about 2 mm narrower.

source.title: Meet Your Pupilometer – 20/20 Magazine

stem: A patient has a latent phoria that may shift one eye during PD measurement. What is good pupillometer practice?
choices: Measure near PD only
Skip the pupillometer and use the frame PD
Take only a binocular reading with both eyes open
Take monocular readings using the occlusion bar and note any differences
explanation: Without fusion locked in, a phoria can shift one eye. Occluding each eye in turn for monocular readings shows whether the measurement changes.

source.title: Meet Your Pupilometer – 20/20 Magazine

stem: With the patient's eyes closed, a distometer reads 11 mm from the back of the lens to the lid. What vertex distance do you record?
choices: 13 mm
10 mm
11 mm
12 mm
explanation: The distometer contacts the closed lid, so add about 1 mm for lid thickness: 11 + 1 = 12 mm.

source.title: Measuring Vertex: Distometer – 20/20 Magazine

stem: Which pliers are used to change a frame's pantoscopic tilt and to equalize temple heights?
choices: Snipe-nose pliers
Strapping pliers
Angling pliers
Lens axis (turning) pliers
explanation: Angling pliers grip at the endpiece and angle the temple relative to the front. That changes pantoscopic or retroscopic tilt and corrects uneven temples.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: Using round/flat (snipe) pliers to bend a pad arm, which jaw goes on the inside of the bend?
choices: The round jaw
Either jaw; it makes no difference
Neither; pad arms are bent with angling pliers only
The flat jaw
explanation: Putting the round jaw on the inside of the bend gives the metal a radius to curve around instead of a sharp crease, so the pad arm isn't cut or weakened.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: What are European (cup-jaw) nose pad pliers designed to do?
choices: Cut temple screws flush
Grip screw-in or push-in pads by fitting a cup over the pad box while the other jaw rests on the pad face
Turn a lens in its eyewire
Widen a plastic bridge
explanation: The cup-shaped jaw fits over the pad's screw or box assembly, so the pad angle can be adjusted without crushing it.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: A flat-top segment is slightly tilted in a full-rim frame. Which tool lets you rotate the lens without removing it?
choices: Bridge-narrowing pliers
Snipe-nose pliers
Angling pliers
Lens axis (lens turning) pliers with rubber-padded jaws
explanation: Lens axis pliers have large rubber pads that grip both lens surfaces, so you can turn the lens in the eyewire to realign the cylinder axis or segment line.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: A rimless lens has worked loose because its mounting straps have spread wider than the lens is thick. Which pliers address this?
choices: Cutting pliers
European pad pliers
Strapping pliers
Angling pliers
explanation: Strapping pliers have overlapping flat jaws that press the straps back parallel and snug against the lens surfaces.

source.title: Optician's Hand Tools for Frame Adjustments – Bristal Optical

stem: What did the cited studies find about PD measurement repeatability with different methods?
choices: Ruler measurements varied by almost 3 mm between opticians, while digital systems varied by about 0.1–0.25 mm
Digital systems varied by about 3 mm
Pupillometers varied more than rulers
Rulers and digital systems agreed within 0.1 mm
explanation: Rulers depend heavily on the operator. Digital centration systems are far more consistent from one operator to the next, which matters for progressives and free-form lenses.

source.title: Taking the Measure of Digital Centration Systems – 20/20 Magazine CE

stem: Besides PD and fitting height, which measurements do digital centration systems capture to personalize free-form lenses?
choices: Lens material index and Abbe value
Vertex distance, pantoscopic tilt, and frame wrap in the chosen frame
Intraocular pressure and pupil reaction
Corneal curvature and tear breakup time
explanation: These position-of-wear values let the lab compensate a digital design for how the frame actually sits on the patient's face.

source.title: Taking the Measure of Digital Centration Systems – 20/20 Magazine CE

stem: What should be done before taking measurements with a digital centration device?
choices: Set the frame to zero pantoscopic tilt
Dilate the patient's pupils
Remove the demo lenses' markings with alcohol
Adjust the chosen frame so it fits the patient properly
explanation: The device measures the frame as worn. If the frame is out of adjustment, it records the wrong fitting values.

source.title: Taking the Measure of Digital Centration Systems – 20/20 Magazine CE

stem: How is reading material positioned with a hand-held magnifier?
choices: At the magnifier's focal point, used with the patient's distance correction
Touching the lens, used with a bifocal
Inside the focal length, used with a strong reading add
Beyond twice the focal length, used without glasses
explanation: At the focal point, light leaving the magnifier is parallel, so the image appears to come from infinity. The patient views it through their distance Rx.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Why does a stand magnifier usually require the patient to accommodate or wear a reading add?
choices: Stand magnifiers are always minus lenses
The stand holds the lens beyond its focal length, so the image is real and inverted
The print sits inside the lens's focal length, so the virtual image is at a finite distance and light leaving the lens diverges
The illumination constricts the pupil
explanation: Because the image isn't at infinity, the eye must focus for a near distance. That takes accommodation or an add.

source.title: Low-Vision Aids – American Academy of Ophthalmology

stem: A patient asks for the largest, strongest hand magnifier available. What should you explain?
choices: Diameter has no relation to power
The larger the lens diameter, the weaker the power tends to be
Larger magnifiers are always stronger
Large magnifiers are only available as stand magnifiers
explanation: Strong magnifiers have steep curves and short focal lengths, which limits their diameter. Big lenses come in lower powers.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Which describes a Galilean telescope used as a low vision aid?
choices: A plus objective and minus eyepiece, typically 2×–4×, lighter and shorter with an erect image
Two plus lenses with an inverting prism, typically 6×–10×
A single high-plus lens mounted in a half-eye
A minus objective and plus eyepiece, used only for near
explanation: Galilean scopes are compact and inexpensive with a larger exit pupil. Keplerian scopes use two plus lenses, need a prism to erect the image, and are longer and heavier.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Why does a Keplerian (astronomical) telescope used as a low vision aid need a prism system?
choices: To correct the patient's astigmatism
To add base-in prism for convergence
Its two plus lenses form an inverted image that must be re-erected
To reduce its weight
explanation: Two plus lenses produce an inverted image. An erecting prism turns it right side up, which adds length, weight, and cost.

source.title: Low-Vision Aids – American Academy of Ophthalmology

stem: What is a bioptic telescope?
choices: A telescope mounted in the reading segment for near work
A small telescope mounted high in a spectacle carrier lens, so the patient looks through the regular lens and dips the head to spot through the telescope
A hand-held monocular with an autofocus lens
Two telescopes cemented together for binocular use
explanation: Mounting the telescope in the upper part of the lens keeps the wide field of the carrier lens for walking. The telescope is used briefly for distance detail.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Using the common prescribing rule of add power plus 2Δ base-in per eye, how much prism goes in a binocular +10.00 D reading spectacle?
choices: 6Δ base in, each eye
12Δ base out, each eye
10Δ base in, each eye
12Δ base in, each eye
explanation: The rule is add + 2Δ base in for each eye. With +10.00 D that is 12Δ BI per eye, which reduces the heavy convergence demand at the close working distance.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: What should patients be told about high-power prismatic half-eye readers?
choices: They work best for driving
They should be worn full time
They are for reading only, not for walking around
They replace the distance prescription
explanation: These lenses focus at a short working distance, so the world beyond it is blurred. They are for seated near tasks only.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: A microscopic spectacle lens has an equivalent power of +32 D. Using the conventional rating, what is its magnification?
explanation: Microscopic spectacles are rated by dividing the dioptric power by 4: 32 ÷ 4 = 8×.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: Up to about what add power can high-plus reading spectacles still be prescribed binocularly?
choices: About +20 D
Any power, if base-out prism is added
About +4 D
About +10 D
explanation: AAO notes high-plus spectacles can be prescribed binocularly up to about 10 D. Beyond that, the convergence demand makes monocular use the norm.

source.title: Low-Vision Aids – American Academy of Ophthalmology

stem: What is another name for a telemicroscope?
choices: Reading telescope or surgical loupe
Bioptic carrier
Stand magnifier
Fresnel prism
explanation: A telemicroscope is a telescope focused for near, by a reading cap or by focusing. It gives a longer working distance than a simple high-plus lens of the same magnification.

source.title: Optical and Low Tech Devices – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: How does the FDA classify a low-vision magnifier, whether hand-held or spectacle-mounted?
choices: Class I, exempt from premarket notification
Not regulated as a medical device
Class II, requiring 510(k) clearance
Class III, requiring premarket approval
explanation: 21 CFR 886.5540 places low-vision magnifiers in Class I (general controls) and exempts them from 510(k) premarket notification.

source.title: 21 CFR 886.5540 – Low-vision magnifier (eCFR)

stem: What power range are over-the-counter reading glasses typically sold in?
explanation: Ready readers cover common reading powers from about +0.75 to +3.50 D, with the same power in both lenses.

source.title: Corrective lens (Reading glasses) – Wikipedia

stem: Which patient is the poorest candidate for ready-made readers?
choices: A patient who wants a spare pair for occasional reading
A patient who wants half-eye readers to look over for distance
An emmetropic presbyope who needs +1.50 at near
A presbyope with significant astigmatism or a large difference in power between the eyes
explanation: OTC readers have equal spherical powers and a standard centration. They don't correct astigmatism or anisometropia, so these patients need a custom Rx.

source.title: Corrective lens (Reading glasses) – Wikipedia

stem: Must over-the-counter reading glasses meet the FDA impact-resistance requirement?
choices: No; only prescription lenses must be impact resistant
Only if they are sold with a case
Yes; 21 CFR 801.410 applies to nonprescription eyeglasses, and their lenses may be tested by statistically significant batch sampling
Only if they are made of glass
explanation: 801.410 covers eyeglasses and sunglasses generally. It specifically allows nonprescription lenses to be batch-tested on a statistical basis in finished or uncut-finished form.

source.title: 21 CFR 801.410 – Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses (eCFR)

stem: What is the practical advantage of half-eye readers over full-frame readers?
choices: The wearer can look over the top for distance without removing them
They provide a wider reading field
They correct astigmatism
They give more magnification at the same power
explanation: Half-eyes sit low on the nose. Full-frame readers must be removed to see clearly at distance.

source.title: Corrective lens (Reading glasses) – Wikipedia

stem: How does free-form (digital) surfacing produce a lens surface?
choices: The lens is cast in a mold with the full Rx on the front
A computer-controlled generator cuts the surface point by point to a file of x, y, z coordinates
Abrasive laps of fixed curvature grind the surface, then fine it
A laser ablates the back surface to the prescribed curve
explanation: Digital generators follow a surface data file. That allows complex shapes and power accuracy to about 0.01 D instead of the tenth-of-a-diopter steps of conventional surfacing.

source.title: Digital Lens Surfacing: The Time is Now – Coburn Technologies

stem: Compared with conventional surfacing, about how precise can free-form lens power be?
choices: About 0.12 D
About 0.50 D
About 0.25 D
About 0.01 D
explanation: HOYA cites conventional accuracy near 1/10 D, versus about 1/100 D for free-form.

source.title: Understanding Free Form vs. Conventional – HOYA Vision Care

stem: Why is conventional surfacing limited to spherical and toric curves?
choices: Only spherical curves can be polished to a clear finish
Conventional generators can only cut convex surfaces
The lap fining step uses fixed-curvature tools, which can only reproduce circular (spherical or toric) surfaces
Spherical curves are required by ANSI Z80.1
explanation: In conventional processing the generated surface is fined and polished on laps. Those laps restrict the result to circular curves. Free-form cuts smooth enough to skip laps, so aspheric, atoric, and progressive back surfaces are possible.

source.title: The Other Side of Free-Form – 20/20 Magazine

stem: Why can a digital surfacing lab keep a much smaller lens inventory than a conventional lab?
choices: It needs only one base curve for all powers
It outsources all progressive work
It can generate the progressive design and Rx on the back of an inexpensive single-vision blank
It buys finished lenses for every Rx
explanation: Conventional progressives require stocking molded front-surface progressive blanks in many base curves and adds. Free-form cuts the progressive onto the back of a single-vision semi-finished blank.

source.title: Digital Lens Surfacing: The Time is Now – Coburn Technologies

stem: What is the main tradeoff of polishing the exposed edges of rimless or semi-rimless lenses?
choices: They look cleaner and less visible, but some wearers notice rainbows or internal reflections
They block more UV but scratch more easily
They make the lens thinner but change its power
They become more impact resistant but heavier
explanation: A polished edge removes the chalky white ring. It can also send stray light into the lens, which some wearers see as rings or rainbows, especially at night. AR coating reduces this.

source.title: Polished Lens Edges, Friend or Foe? – 20/20 Magazine

stem: What does "rolling" a lens edge do, and when is it typically needed?
choices: It reduces the C-size so the lens fits a smaller frame
It fines down the sharp edge, mainly on high-minus lenses or when the edge interferes with temple closure or a pad arm
It adds a safety bevel required on all dress lenses
It thins the center of a high-plus lens
explanation: Rolling bevels the sharp corner of a thick edge. It makes the edge look thinner and clears parts that bump it. It is often paired with polish.

source.title: Living on the Edge – Eyecare Business

stem: How does a dark edge coating help a thick high-minus lens?
choices: It reduces the actual edge thickness
It lowers the effective power
It strengthens the lens for safety use
It makes the edge less visible against the frame, and it does not change the lens power or thickness
explanation: Edge coatings seal or pigment the cut edge. They hide the thickness visually but leave the lens optics unchanged.

source.title: Edge Coating/Polishing for High Prescriptions – Specialty Vision

stem: For a high-minus patient, which frame choice does the most to reduce edge thickness and weight?
choices: Any frame, provided the lenses are high-index
A rimless frame with polished edges
A large frame with a flat base curve
A frame that holds physically small lenses
explanation: Smaller lenses use less of the surface sphere, so a minus lens ends with a thinner edge. A 40 mm lens can weigh about half as much as a 50 mm one.

source.title: Corrective lens (Reading glasses) – Wikipedia

stem: Under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, what does "universal precautions" mean?
choices: Wearing gloves only when blood is visible
Vaccinating all patients before treatment
Treating all human blood and certain body fluids as if known to be infectious
Disinfecting only items used on patients known to be infected
explanation: OSHA defines universal precautions as an approach in which all human blood and certain body fluids are treated as if infectious for HIV, HBV, and other bloodborne pathogens.

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 – Bloodborne pathogens (OSHA)

stem: Under OSHA 1910.1030, when must hepatitis B vaccination be made available to an employee with occupational exposure?
choices: After required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment
Within one year of hire
Only after an exposure incident
Only if the employee requests it in writing
explanation: The employer must offer the vaccine series within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee is already vaccinated, is immune, or has a medical contraindication.

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 – Bloodborne pathogens (OSHA)

stem: How often must an employer's bloodborne pathogens Exposure Control Plan be reviewed and updated?
choices: Every five years
At least annually, and whenever tasks or positions with exposure change
Only after an OSHA inspection
Only when a new employee is hired
explanation: OSHA requires review at least annually and whenever new or modified tasks or positions affect occupational exposure.

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 – Bloodborne pathogens (OSHA)

stem: CDC standard precautions apply to which patients?
choices: Only patients with open wounds
All patients, in all patient care
Only patients with a known infection
Only patients undergoing surgery
explanation: Standard precautions are the baseline for all patient care: hand hygiene, PPE when exposure is expected, respiratory etiquette, and cleaning and disinfecting equipment and the environment.

source.title: Standard Precautions for All Patient Care – CDC

stem: Under the Spaulding classification, frames, pupillometers, and hand tools that touch only intact skin are:
choices: Critical items requiring sterilization
Semicritical items requiring high-level disinfection
Noncritical items requiring low-level disinfection
Exempt from any cleaning
explanation: Noncritical items contact intact skin but not mucous membranes. Intact skin is an effective barrier, so low-level disinfection is appropriate.

source.title: A Rational Approach to Disinfection and Sterilization – CDC

stem: Under the Spaulding classification, a device that contacts mucous membranes, such as the conjunctiva, is:
choices: Semicritical, requiring at least high-level disinfection
Exempt if used on only one patient per day
Noncritical, requiring low-level disinfection
Critical, requiring sterilization
explanation: Semicritical items contact mucous membranes or nonintact skin. They must be free of all microorganisms except small numbers of bacterial spores, which means high-level disinfection at minimum.

source.title: A Rational Approach to Disinfection and Sterilization – CDC

stem: When an optical office disinfects counters and tools with a hospital disinfectant, what does federal law require?
choices: Label contact times are only suggestions
The product must be FDA-approved as a drug
Any household cleaner may be used if it is diluted
The product must be EPA-registered, and all label directions, including contact time, must be followed
explanation: EPA registers disinfectants under FIFRA. CDC notes that federal law requires users to follow all label instructions, such as use-dilution, contact time, storage, and disposal.

source.title: A Rational Approach to Disinfection and Sterilization – CDC

stem: Under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, what must an optical lab provide to workers who handle hazardous chemicals such as tints, solvents, and coating chemicals?
choices: A signed liability waiver
Only a verbal warning from the supervisor
Labels and safety data sheets, plus training on the hazards
Annual hepatitis B testing
explanation: All employers with hazardous chemicals in the workplace must have labels and safety data sheets for exposed workers and must train them to handle the chemicals appropriately.

source.title: Hazard Communication – OSHA

stem: Under the current OSHA Hazard Communication Standard, aligned with GHS, how is a safety data sheet (SDS) organized?
choices: However the manufacturer prefers
As a free-form one-page summary
In an 8-section format
In a specified 16-section format
explanation: The HCS adopted the Globally Harmonized System, which specifies a 16-section SDS and harmonized label elements: signal word, pictogram, and hazard statement.

source.title: Hazard Communication – OSHA

stem: Under 21 CFR 801.410, how long must invoices and records of sale for impact-resistant lenses be kept?
choices: 3 years
7 years
1 year
5 years
explanation: Shipping and sales records for impact-resistant lenses, including finished eyeglasses and sunglasses, must be kept for 3 years. Retailers need not record the names of nonprescription purchasers.

source.title: 21 CFR 801.410 – Use of impact-resistant lenses in eyeglasses and sunglasses (eCFR)

stem: In the National Academy of Opticianry's liability analysis, what is an optician who mounts uncut lenses into frames considered?
choices: The lens manufacturer's agent, covered by its testing
The manufacturer, legally responsible for the finished eyewear
A distributor with no liability
Exempt, as long as the prescriber signed the Rx
explanation: NAO points out that an optician who edges and assembles lenses is the manufacturer under FDA rules. Processing beyond simple edging and tinting can remove the protection of the lens maker's batch testing.

source.title: Professional Liability for Opticians, Part I – National Academy of Opticianry

stem: What is the core of the optician's "duty to warn"?
choices: Posting the FDA drop-ball test procedure in the office
Refusing to dispense any lens other than polycarbonate
Informing patients about the relative impact resistance of lens materials so they can make an informed choice, and documenting that they were told
Warning patients that all lenses are shatterproof
explanation: The duty to warn rests on informed choice. Patients must know that some materials, such as polycarbonate, resist impact better. The patient record should note that the information was given.

source.title: Protecting Kids (and others) through 'Duty to Warn' – Eyecare Business

stem: Which group of patients is most often cited as needing a recommendation of impact-resistant lenses like polycarbonate?
choices: Children, industrial workers, police and fire personnel, and sports participants
Only patients who buy sunglasses
Only patients with high-minus prescriptions
Only patients over age 65
explanation: These groups are the most likely to have their eyewear struck. Many offices insist on polycarbonate for children.

source.title: Protecting Kids (and others) through 'Duty to Warn' – Eyecare Business

stem: In product liability law, when a product's users weren't told what it can and can't do, what kind of defect is that?
choices: Manufacturing defect
Defective warning
Breach of express warranty
Design defect
explanation: NAO lists three defect areas. A manufacturing defect doesn't match its design, a design defect is a flawed design, and a defective warning means effective instructions or warnings were missing.

source.title: Professional Liability for Opticians, Part I – National Academy of Opticianry

stem: A patient tells the optician the glasses are for racquetball, and the optician supplies dress eyewear that fails in play. Which legal concept most directly applies?
choices: Express warranty
Implied warranty of merchantability
Strict liability for prescribers only
Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
explanation: When a buyer relies on the seller's expertise for a specific use, the goods are implied to be fit for that purpose. Opticians have a duty to ask how the eyewear will be used.

source.title: Professional Liability for Opticians, Part I – National Academy of Opticianry

stem: What is wrong with putting safety-thickness lenses in a dress frame for a patient who needs protective eyewear?
choices: Nothing; lens thickness alone defines safety eyewear
The FDA prohibits safety lenses in any dress frame
The patient needs protection, but the frame doesn't provide it, which is hard to defend if the eyewear fails
Dress frames can't hold 3 mm lenses
explanation: NAO points out that recognizing a patient needs extra lens protection but not frame protection is awkward to defend. Protective eyewear is a lens-and-frame system.

source.title: Professional Liability for Opticians, Part I – National Academy of Opticianry

stem: For basketball and soccer, which standard should sports eye guards be certified to?
choices: ASTM F803
ANSI Z87.1
ANSI Z80.3
explanation: Prevent Blindness recommends eye guards approved to ASTM F803 (or the current sport-specific ASTM standard), with polycarbonate lenses. Racket sports now use ASTM F3164.

source.title: Recommended Sports Eye Protectors – Prevent Blindness Texas

stem: For racquetball and squash, which ASTM standard does Prevent Blindness currently recommend for eye guards?
choices: ASTM F2713
ASTM F3164
ASTM F803 only
ASTM F3077
explanation: Racket sports have their own standard, F3164. F2713 covers field hockey and F3077 covers women's lacrosse.

source.title: Recommended Sports Eye Protectors – Prevent Blindness Texas

stem: According to FDA guidance, which claim may a nonprescription sunglass make if it meets the UV requirements of ANSI Z80.3?
choices: That it blocks 100% of all UV regardless of testing
That it prevents macular degeneration
That it replaces the need for a hat
That its lenses meet ANSI Z80.3 UV-blocking requirements, optionally stating the percentage of UVB and UVA blocked
explanation: FDA guidance allows labeling that references ANSI Z80.3 UV requirements and percentage blocked. FDA has taken exception to unsubstantiated performance claims.

source.title: Guidance Document for Nonprescription Sunglasses – FDA

stem: Which wavelength band is generally meant by "high-energy visible" (HEV) light?
choices: About 280–315 nm, UVB
About 315–380 nm, UVA
About 400–450 nm, violet-blue
About 600–700 nm, red
explanation: HEV refers to short-wave visible light in the violet-blue band, roughly 400 to 450 nm, just beyond the UV range.

source.title: High-energy visible light – Wikipedia

stem: When discussing blue-light filters with a computer user, which statement reflects the American Academy of Ophthalmology's position?
choices: Screens emit more blue light than the sun
There's no scientific evidence that blue light from screens damages the eye, and the AAO doesn't recommend blue-blocking eyewear for computer use
Blue-light filters cure digital eye strain
Blue-light filters are proven to prevent macular degeneration
explanation: AAO attributes screen discomfort mainly to digital eye strain from reduced blinking. Sunlight is the largest source of blue light. Accurate product claims are part of the duty to warn.

source.title: Should You Be Worried About Blue Light? – American Academy of Ophthalmology

stem: Which CPT code reports fitting of monofocal (single-vision) spectacles for a patient without aphakia?
explanation: 92340 = monofocal fitting; 92341 = bifocal; 92342 = multifocal other than bifocal; 92352/92353 = aphakic spectacle prosthesis fitting.

source.title: Eyeglass Lenses – Medi-Cal Provider Manual

stem: Which CPT code reports fitting of trifocal or progressive (multifocal, other than bifocal) spectacles for a patient without aphakia?
explanation: 92342 is "fitting of spectacles, except for aphakia; multifocal, other than bifocal." 92353 is the multifocal code for aphakia.

source.title: Eyeglass Lenses – Medi-Cal Provider Manual

stem: Which CPT codes cover fitting of spectacle-mounted low vision aids?
choices: 92354 (single-element system) and 92355 (telescopic or other compound lens system)
explanation: 92354 is for a single-element system and 92355 for a telescopic or compound lens system. 92370/92371 are repair and refitting.

source.title: Vision Care Procedure Codes – eMedNY (NY Medicaid)

stem: A patient (not aphakic) brings in glasses for repair and refitting. Which CPT code describes this service?
explanation: 92370 is repair and refitting of spectacles except for aphakia. 92371 is the same service for an aphakic spectacle prosthesis.

source.title: Vision Care Procedure Codes – eMedNY (NY Medicaid)

stem: Which HCPCS code describes a progressive lens?
choices: V2100, per lens
V2020, per frame
V2750, per lens
V2781, per lens
explanation: V2781 = progressive lens, per lens. V2020 = frames, purchases. V2100 = single-vision sphere, plano to ±4.00. V2750 = anti-reflective coating.

source.title: HCPCS 'V' Codes – HCPCSData.com

stem: Which pair correctly matches HCPCS V-codes with lens add-ons?
choices: V2784 = polycarbonate lens; V2744 = photochromatic tint
V2784 = progressive lens; V2744 = scratch coating
V2784 = frame, deluxe; V2744 = UV coating
V2784 = anti-reflective coating; V2744 = polarization
explanation: V2784 is lens, polycarbonate or equal, per lens. V2744 is tint, photochromatic, per lens. V2750 is AR, V2755 is UV, V2760 is scratch-resistant coating.

source.title: HCPCS 'V' Codes – HCPCSData.com

stem: After cataract surgery with an intraocular lens, what does Medicare Part B cover?
choices: A new pair of eyeglasses every year
Nothing; Medicare never covers eyewear
Unlimited replacements for one year
One pair of eyeglasses with standard frames (or one set of contact lenses) after each cataract surgery
explanation: Medicare doesn't cover routine eyewear. It does pay for one pair of glasses with standard frames, or contacts, after each cataract surgery that implants an IOL, from a Medicare-enrolled supplier.

source.title: Eyeglasses & contact lenses – Medicare.gov

stem: A Medicare post-cataract patient wants progressive lenses and AR coating that Medicare treats as noncovered upgrades. What should the dispensary do?
choices: Have the patient sign a general waiver saying 'Medicare may not pay'
Bill the upgrades as standard lenses
Have the patient sign an Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) before dispensing and append modifier GA to the claim
Refuse to sell the upgrades
explanation: The ABN must be completed and reviewed with the patient beforehand. A general statement is not acceptable, and claims with an ABN on file carry modifier GA.

source.title: Learn to Code Optical Dispensing – American Academy of Ophthalmology

stem: What is a frame "allowance" in a vision plan?
choices: The maximum frame size the plan covers
A set dollar amount the plan pays toward a frame; the patient pays any difference
A copay for the eye exam
A discount on contact lenses only
explanation: Plans typically pay up to an allowance for frames and lenses within a benefit period, often every one to two years. The patient pays the overage.

source.title: Vision insurance: A guide to plans, costs and benefits – All About Vision

stem: A patient on a vision plan is diagnosed with glaucoma. Which coverage generally pays for diagnosing and treating the disease?
choices: The patient's medical (health) insurance
Neither; eye disease is never covered
The vision plan's lens benefit
The vision plan's frame allowance
explanation: Vision plans cover routine exams and eyewear. Medical insurance covers diagnosis and treatment of eye diseases, conditions, and injuries.

source.title: Vision insurance: A guide to plans, costs and benefits – All About Vision

stem: What is the difference between an electronic medical record (EMR) and an electronic health record (EHR)?
choices: An EMR is a practice's digital chart for its own encounters, while an EHR is a broader, longitudinal record that can draw on multiple EMRs
An EMR is a paper chart that has been scanned
An EHR stores only billing data
They are legally distinct; only an EHR is covered by HIPAA
explanation: The terms are often used interchangeably, but an EMR is the provider's encounter record within a practice and can serve as a data source for an EHR. Both are subject to HIPAA security requirements.

source.title: Electronic health record – Wikipedia

stem: What is nystagmus?
choices: A latent turning tendency revealed by covering one eye
Involuntary, repetitive eye movement
Absence of the crystalline lens
A blind spot surrounded by normal vision
explanation: Nystagmus is an involuntary (occasionally voluntary) to-and-fro eye movement. It may be congenital or acquired and often reduces vision.

source.title: Nystagmus – Wikipedia

stem: In jerk nystagmus, how are the two phases of the movement described?
choices: Two equal-speed swings, like a pendulum
Two slow phases with no fast phase
A slow drift in one direction followed by a fast corrective movement; the nystagmus is named for the fast phase
Only a fast phase, with no drift
explanation: Equal-speed oscillation is pendular nystagmus. Jerk nystagmus has a slow drift and a quick return, and its direction is named by the quick phase.

source.title: Nystagmus – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: A patient with nystagmus habitually turns the head to one side. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: Aniseikonia from unequal lenses
A scotoma in the central field
A tropia that needs base-down prism
Their null point, where the nystagmus is least, lies away from primary gaze
explanation: When the gaze direction that dampens the nystagmus is off to one side, patients turn the head to put the eyes there. Keep this in mind when fitting and measuring.

source.title: Nystagmus – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: For nystagmus that dampens with convergence, what kind of prism may be prescribed?
choices: Yoked base-down prism
Base-out prism, to stimulate convergence
Base-in prism, to relax convergence
Base-up prism over both eyes
explanation: Base-out prism makes the eyes converge. When convergence dampens the nystagmus, as in infantile idiopathic nystagmus, this can steady the eyes.

source.title: Nystagmus – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: What is a scotoma?
choices: Double vision
Involuntary eye movement
A difference in image size between the eyes
An area of reduced or lost vision surrounded by relatively normal vision
explanation: Every eye has a physiological scotoma, the blind spot at the optic disc. Pathological scotomas can result from macular degeneration, optic nerve disease, or brain injury.

source.title: Scotoma – Wikipedia

stem: What are the main optical consequences of aphakia, the absence of the crystalline lens?
choices: Astigmatism only, with no change in sphere
Presbyopia that reverses itself
High hyperopia and total loss of accommodation
High myopia with normal accommodation
explanation: Removing the lens takes away a large share of the eye's plus power and all ability to accommodate. Before IOLs, this was corrected with thick high-plus cataract spectacles.

source.title: Aphakia – Wikipedia

stem: A pseudophakic patient has a standard monofocal IOL set for distance. What will they most likely still need?
choices: Reading glasses or an add for near work, because the IOL can't accommodate
A high-plus cataract lens for distance
Base-in prism for distance
No correction at any distance
explanation: Most IOLs are fixed monofocal lenses matched to distance. Without accommodation, near work needs plus, unless a multifocal or EDOF IOL was used.

source.title: Intraocular lens – Wikipedia

stem: What distinguishes a phoria from a tropia?
choices: A phoria causes constant diplopia; a tropia never does
A phoria occurs only at near; a tropia only at distance
A phoria is a latent deviation held in check by fusion; a tropia is a manifest misalignment present with both eyes open
A phoria is always vertical; a tropia is always horizontal
explanation: A heterophoria appears only when fusion is broken, for example by covering one eye. Strabismus (a tropia) is a misalignment while the patient is trying to fixate with both eyes.

source.title: Heterophoria – Wikipedia

stem: What is the term for a latent tendency of the eyes to turn outward when fusion is broken?
choices: Exophoria
Exotropia
Esophoria
Hyperphoria
explanation: Exo- means outward and -phoria means latent. Esophoria is a latent inward tendency, hyperphoria is vertical, and exotropia is a manifest outward turn.

source.title: Heterophoria – Wikipedia

stem: When prism is prescribed to help an esotropic (inward-turning) eye, which base direction is typically used?
choices: Base up
Base out
Base in
Base down
explanation: Prism moves the image toward its apex. Base-out prism shifts the image inward, to where the esotropic eye is pointing. Exotropia takes base in.

source.title: Manual Lensometry – OSMA Ophthalmic Skills Workshop

stem: A patient's double vision persists with one eye covered. How is it classified?
choices: Decompensated phoria
Binocular diplopia
Physiological diplopia
Monocular diplopia
explanation: Diplopia that persists with one eye closed is monocular and points to a problem within that eye. Binocular diplopia disappears when either eye is covered.

source.title: Diplopia – Wikipedia

stem: What happens to the eyes when a person shifts fixation from a distant object to a near one?
choices: They make a vertical vergence movement
They converge (rotate toward each other), together with accommodation
They stay parallel while only the pupils constrict
They diverge until the lines of sight are parallel
explanation: Near fixation drives convergence, and distance fixation drives divergence toward parallel lines of sight. Vergence is closely linked with accommodation.

source.title: Vergence – Wikipedia

stem: At what refractive difference between the two eyes is anisometropia generally diagnosed?
choices: About 0.25 diopter
About 5 diopters
About 10 diopters
About 1 diopter
explanation: A 1 D difference is the usual threshold. Many patients tolerate up to about 3 D before symptoms like headache, eyestrain, or diplopia appear.

source.title: Anisometropia – Wikipedia

stem: Why is uncorrected anisometropia in early childhood a concern?
choices: It permanently paralyzes accommodation
It produces a scotoma at the optic disc
The brain may suppress the more blurred eye, leading to amblyopia
It always causes a cataract
explanation: When one image is consistently poorer during visual development, the cortex suppresses it. That can leave the eye amblyopic even after correction.

source.title: Anisometropia – Wikipedia

stem: Before IOLs, why was cataract removal in only one eye a classic cause of aniseikonia when corrected with spectacles?
choices: The operated eye became highly hyperopic, creating a large anisometropia whose spectacle correction produced very unequal image sizes
The operated eye became highly myopic and needed a minus lenticular
Removing the lens shrank the retina in the operated eye
The crystalline lens of the other eye magnified images
explanation: Without its crystalline lens the eye is strongly hyperopic. Correcting one aphakic eye with a high-plus spectacle lens next to a normal fellow eye creates marked anisometropia and image-size difference. IOLs largely solved this.

source.title: Aniseikonia – Wikipedia

stem: What is antimetropia?
choices: Both eyes are equally myopic
The two eyes see images of different sizes
One eye has astigmatism and the other is spherical
One eye is myopic and the other is hyperopic
explanation: Antimetropia is a rare subtype of anisometropia, about 0.1% of people, with opposite-sign refractive errors.

source.title: Anisometropia – Wikipedia

stem: What is aniseikonia?
choices: A difference in accommodation between the eyes
A significant difference in the perceived image size between the two eyes
A vertical misalignment of the eyes
A difference in pupil size between the eyes
explanation: Aniseikonia can be an overall or a meridional size difference. It is often induced by spectacle correction of anisometropia.

source.title: Aniseikonia – Wikipedia

stem: Using the clinical rule of thumb, about how much aniseikonia is expected when spectacles correct OD −1.00 and OS −4.50?
choices: About 3.5%
About 1%
About 5.5%
About 10%
explanation: Spectacle-corrected anisometropia produces about 1% aniseikonia per diopter. The difference here is 3.50 D, so about 3.5%.

source.title: Aniseikonia – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: According to Knapp's rule, when anisometropia is corrected with spectacles, which type produces less aniseikonia?
choices: Refractive anisometropia
Both produce the same aniseikonia
Axial anisometropia
Neither; spectacles do not change image size
explanation: Knapp's rule: with spectacle correction, axial anisometropia produces less aniseikonia than refractive anisometropia. The reverse is true with contact lenses. In practice, non-optical factors such as retinal stretching in long myopic eyes also contribute.

source.title: Aniseikonia – EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

stem: Which spectacle lens parameters can be adjusted to change magnification and reduce aniseikonia?
choices: Base curve, center thickness, and vertex distance
Add power and segment height only
Abbe value and lens index only
Tint, coating, and frame color
explanation: The shape factor (front curve and thickness) and the power factor (power and vertex) together set spectacle magnification. Iseikonic designs adjust them to equalize image size.

source.title: Aniseikonia – Wikipedia

stem: Antimetropic bifocal wearer: OD −2.00 D, OS +2.00 D, both spheres. Reading 8 mm below the optical centers, how much vertical imbalance is induced?
choices: 0Δ
explanation: OD: 2.00 × 0.8 = 1.6Δ base down (minus lens, below the OC). OS: 2.00 × 0.8 = 1.6Δ base up (plus lens, below the OC). Opposite base directions add, so the imbalance is 3.2Δ.

source.title: Plus Cylinder Lensometry – University of Iowa Ophthalmology

stem: In hand neutralization, a target seen through an unknown lens moves in the same direction as the lens ("with" motion). What does this indicate?
choices: Prism with no power
A spherical lens with no cylinder
Plus power in that meridian; neutralize it with minus trial lenses
Minus power in that meridian; neutralize it with plus trial lenses
explanation: With motion means minus and against motion means plus. Stack trial lenses of the opposite sign until the motion stops. The unknown power is equal and opposite to the neutralizing lens.

source.title: Lens Neutralisation by Hand – Eyedocs

stem: During hand neutralization, rotating the unknown lens makes the image of a cross appear to "scissor." What does this reveal?
choices: The lens is spherical
The lens is a bifocal
The lens has cylinder; the principal meridians are where the image lines line up with the object cross
The lens has prism but no power
explanation: Scissoring means astigmatic power. Rotate until the image lines are perpendicular and continuous with the object lines, then mark those principal meridians and neutralize each separately.

source.title: Lens Neutralisation by Hand – Eyedocs

stem: Hand neutralizing an unknown lens: the vertical meridian is neutralized by a −1.50 D trial lens and the horizontal meridian by a −0.50 D trial lens. What is the lens power?
explanation: The lens is equal and opposite to the neutralizers: +1.50 at 90 and +0.50 at 180. In minus-cylinder form, sphere = the more plus meridian (+1.50), cylinder = −1.00, and the axis is that meridian (090).

source.title: Lens Neutralisation by Hand – Eyedocs

stem: During hand neutralization, the image of the cross can't be brought into line with the object cross no matter how the lens is moved. What does this indicate?
choices: The trial lens is too strong
The lens is a pure cylinder
The lens contains ground-in prism
The lens is plano
explanation: If no position aligns the image with the object, there is no point free of prism. The lens has prism ground in.

source.title: Lens Neutralisation by Hand – Eyedocs

stem: A presbyope fully corrected for distance has 1.00 D of amplitude remaining and wears a +2.00 add. What is the range of clear vision through the add?
choices: About 20 cm to 33 cm
About 33 cm to 50 cm
About 25 cm to 100 cm
About 50 cm to infinity
explanation: Relaxed, the add focuses at 1/2.00 = 50 cm. With full accommodation the total is 3.00 D, which focuses at 1/3.00 ≈ 33 cm.

source.title: The Near Point – AAO Basic Optics, Chapter 9

stem: Using the guideline that half of the amplitude is kept in reserve, what tentative add does a patient with 1.50 D of amplitude need for a 33 cm working distance?
explanation: Demand at 33 cm = 3.00 D. Usable accommodation = ½ × 1.50 = 0.75 D. Tentative add = 3.00 − 0.75 = +2.25.

source.title: Understanding Presbyopia – Journal of Current Research and Studies

stem: By Hofstetter's average formula, what is the expected amplitude of accommodation at age 50?
explanation: Average amplitude = 18.5 − (0.30 × age) = 18.5 − 15 = 3.5 D. Keeping half in reserve leaves about 1.75 D for sustained near work.

source.title: Accommodation (vertebrate eye) – Wikipedia

stem: An uncorrected −3.00 D myope has 4.00 D of accommodation. What is the range of clear vision without glasses?
choices: About 10 cm to 25 cm
About 33 cm to 100 cm
About 14 cm to 33 cm
About 25 cm to infinity
explanation: Far point = 1/3.00 ≈ 33 cm. Full accommodation adds 4.00 D for a total of 7.00 D, so the near point is 1/7 ≈ 14 cm.

source.title: The Near Point – AAO Basic Optics, Chapter 9

stem: An uncorrected +2.00 D hyperope has 5.00 D of accommodation. Where is the near point without glasses?
choices: About 20 cm
About 33 cm
About 14 cm
About 50 cm
explanation: Two diopters of accommodation go to offsetting the hyperopia, which leaves 3.00 D for near: 1/3.00 ≈ 33 cm.

source.title: The Near Point – AAO Basic Optics, Chapter 9
